title: Trauma and emergency imaging

steps.tx: Blunt thoracic aortic injury typically occurs at the **aortic isthmus**, immediately distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery at the attachment of the ligamentum arteriosum. Rapid deceleration fixes the aorta, causing shear tears that manifest on CT as intimal flaps, mediastinal haematoma, active contrast extravasation, or traumatic **pseudoaneurysm**.

left.title: Aortic Isthmus Vulnerability
points: Transition from mobile arch to fixed descending aorta
Attachment site of ligamentum arteriosum
Severe shear stress during rapid horizontal deceleration
Responsible for > 90% of blunt aortic injury cases
Treated with emergent endovascular stent graft (TEVAR)

right.title: Direct CT Signs
points: Displaced intimal flap across lumen
Irregular pseudoaneurysm contour contour deformity
Luminal filling defect from acute thrombus
Active blush of intravenous contrast extravasation
Periaortic mediastinal haematoma

steps.tx: **Boerhaave syndrome** represents spontaneous transmural oesophageal perforation triggered by sudden rises in intraluminal pressure during forceful vomiting. Rupture occurs classically in the left posterolateral distal oesophagus, producing Mackler triad (vomiting, chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema), **pneumomediastinum**, left hydropneumothorax, and water-soluble oral contrast extravasation.

Rupture occurs classically in the left posterolateral distal oesophagus, producing Mackler triad of vomiting, chest pain, and subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum, left hydropneumothorax, and water-soluble oral contrast extravasation.

vis.caption: Pneumomediastinum and distal oesophageal rupture in Boerhaave syndrome

steps.tx: Acute **Epidural haematoma** characteristically arises from laceration of the **middle meningeal artery** secondary to a temporal bone fracture across the pterion. On unenhanced brain CT, it appears as a biconvex, lentiform, high-attenuation extra-axial collection that does not cross cranial sutures because the periosteal dura is firmly anchored at suture lines.

vis.alt: Axial non-contrast CT brain demonstrating biconvex lentiform hyperdense extra-axial epidural haematoma
vis.caption: Biconvex hyperdense collection limited by cranial sutures in epidural haematoma

steps.tx: Acute **Subdural haematoma** results from traumatic deceleration tearing of **bridging cortical veins** as they cross the subdural space to enter the superior sagittal sinus. CT demonstrates a crescent-shaped hyperdense extra-axial collection conforming to the hemispheric convexity, readily crossing cranial sutures while being arrested by the dural reflections of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli.

CT demonstrates a crescent-shaped hyperdense extra-axial collection conforming to the hemispheric convexity, readily crossing cranial sutures while being arrested by the dural reflections of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli.

rows: 3 days to 3 weeks (requires contrast or MRI)

steps.tx: **Diffuse axonal injury** (DAI) is triggered by sudden rotational acceleration-deceleration forces causing axonal shearing. Initial CT often underestimates injury severity, appearing normal or showing petechial microhaemorrhages. T2 gradient-echo or susceptibility-weighted MRI exquisitely demonstrates punctate signal blooming at the grey-white matter junction, **corpus callosum** (splenium), and dorsolateral midbrain.
steps.say: Diffuse axonal injury is triggered by sudden rotational acceleration-deceleration forces causing axonal shearing. Initial CT often underestimates injury severity, appearing normal or showing petechial microhaemorrhages. T2 gradient-echo or susceptibility-weighted MRI exquisitely demonstrates punctate signal blooming at the grey-white matter junction, corpus callosum especially the splenium, and dorsolateral midbrain.

left.title: DAI Anatomical Grading
points: Grade 1: Grey-white matter junction (parasagittal)
Grade 2: Corpus callosum (predominantly splenium)
Grade 3: Dorsolateral midbrain and brainstem
Correlates with profound post-traumatic coma
Permanent axonal retraction ball formation

right.title: MRI Sequence Sensitivity
points: Susceptibility-Weighted Imaging (SWI) most sensitive
Demonstrates susceptibility blooming from paramagnetic blood
Diffusion-Weighted Imaging shows acute cytotoxic swelling
Conventional T1 / T2 markedly underestimates lesions
Explains coma in patients with unremarkable CT

steps.tx: Blunt abdominal trauma uses the **AAST** (American Association for the Surgery of Trauma) organ injury scale for **splenic injury** on CT. Grade 1 involves a capsular tear under 1 cm or subcapsular haematoma under 10% surface area. Grade 4 features active intraperitoneal bleeding or devascularization exceeding 25% of the spleen, while Grade 5 describes a completely shattered, devascularized spleen.
steps.say: Blunt abdominal trauma management relies on the AAST organ injury scale for splenic injury on CT. Grade 1 involves a capsular tear under 1 centimetre or subcapsular haematoma under 10% surface area. Grade 4 features active intraperitoneal bleeding or devascularization exceeding 25% of the spleen, while Grade 5 describes a completely shattered, devascularized spleen.

rows: Laceration > 3 cm depth or trabecular vessel
Subcapsular > 50% area, ruptured or expanding haematoma
Laceration involving segmental or hilar vessels

steps.tx: **Tension pneumothorax** is an immediate clinical and radiological life threat caused by a one-way pleural valve mechanism. Radiographs and CT demonstrate complete ipsilateral lung collapse, severe downward depression of the hemidiaphragm, and marked contralateral **mediastinal shift** and tracheal deviation, which kinks the inferior vena cava and precipitously halts venous return.

left.title: Tension Pneumothorax Signs
points: Complete ipsilateral lung collapse
Contralateral shift of trachea and mediastinum
Inversion and depression of ipsilateral hemidiaphragm
Widening of ipsilateral intercostal spaces
Kinking of IVC with severe haemodynamic collapse

right.title: Simple Pneumothorax Distinction
points: Presence of visible visceral pleural line
Absence of lung markings peripherally
No mediastinal shift or diaphragmatic inversion
Preserved systemic haemodynamic stability
Managed electively or with tube thoracostomy

steps.tx: Unstable **Pelvic fractures** (anteroposterior compression or vertical shear mechanisms) cause catastrophic retroperitoneal haemorrhage from tearing of the posterior sacroiliac ligamentous complex. Severe arterial bleeding originates from branches of the **internal iliac** artery (superior gluteal, internal pudendal, and lateral sacral arteries), alongside extensive low-pressure rupture of the presacral venous plexus.
steps.say: Unstable Pelvic fractures cause catastrophic retroperitoneal haemorrhage from tearing of the posterior sacroiliac ligamentous complex. Severe arterial bleeding originates from branches of the internal iliac artery, especially the superior gluteal, internal pudendal, and lateral sacral arteries, alongside extensive low-pressure rupture of the presacral venous plexus.

rows: Branches of anterior and posterior internal iliac
Pelvic binder stabilization, packing, external fixation
Disrupted sacral and iliac cancellous bone fractures
Mechanical reduction and rigid skeletal fixation
